---
title: "Health status in Portugal"
subtitle: "How long and how well people live, what they die of, which risk factors weigh most, and how access and resources have changed"
lang: en
---

::: {.callout-note}
This report uses only official INE and Eurostat data stored in the repository. Every number,
fact, event or link is marked in the text and has a row in `claims.csv`, with the source, the
access date and a short excerpt. All links between changes in the series and events are grade C:
they indicate coincidence in time, never cause.
:::

```{ojs}
Plotly = require("plotly.js-dist-min@2.35.2")
```

```{ojs}
import {timeSeries, ranking} from "../../assets/charts.js"
```

```{ojs}
lang = "en"
```

```{ojs}
linked_events = FileAttachment("linked_events.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
nuts_regions = ["Portugal", "Norte", "Centro", "Grande Lisboa", "Península de Setúbal", "Oeste e Vale do Tejo", "Alentejo", "Algarve", "Região Autónoma dos Açores", "Região Autónoma da Madeira"]
```

```{ojs}
dedupe = (rows, key) => { const seen = new Set(); return rows.filter((r) => { const k = key(r); if (seen.has(k)) return false; seen.add(k); return true; }); }
```

```{ojs}
region_labels = ({"European Union (27)": "EU-27", "Região Autónoma dos Açores": "Azores", "Região Autónoma da Madeira": "Madeira", "Área Metropolitana de Lisboa": "Lisbon MA"})
```

## Summary

People in Portugal now live longer than at any point in the series: life expectancy at birth rose
from [64.0 years in 1960]{.claim id="c001"} to [82.5 years in 2024]{.claim id="c002"},
[one year above the EU average in 2024]{.claim id="c006"}. The share of that life spent without
limitations also grew: healthy life years at birth rose from [53.9 in 2004]{.claim id="c025"} to
[64.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c026"}, and the gap with the EU narrowed from [9.0 years]{.claim id="c029"}
to [0.4 years]{.claim id="c030"}.

Age-standardised mortality from diseases of the circulatory system fell from
[321.67 deaths per hundred thousand inhabitants in 2011]{.claim id="c040"} to [220.81 in 2023]{.claim id="c041"},
and infant mortality fell from [77.5 per thousand live births in 1960]{.claim id="c082"} to
[3.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c083"}. Mortality from respiratory diseases remains above the European
average ([95.48 against 75.18 per hundred thousand in 2023]{.claim id="c046"}).

There are also less favourable signs. The share of people reporting a chronic condition rose from
[32.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c095"} to [44.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c096"}, partly because of changes in
the survey. Unmet needs for dental care ([7.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c145"}) are more than double the
EU level ([3.3%]{.claim id="c146"}). Household out-of-pocket payments account for
[28.67% of current health expenditure in 2024]{.claim id="c162"}, against
[15.06% in the EU]{.claim id="c163"}.

Automatic detection found [51 candidate breaks in the series, of which 18 were linked to a dated event, all grade C, and 33 were left without an event]{.claim id="c202"}.
None of the exploratory associations between indicators survived correction for multiple testing
([see Associations between indicators]{.claim id="c209"}). Weekly excess mortality during the pandemic was not covered for
lack of a tested source ([see Question 5]{.claim id="c094"}).

## Question 1 — Life expectancy at birth and at 65

Life expectancy at birth in Portugal grew almost continuously from
[1960, when it was 64.0 years]{.claim id="c001"}, to [2024, at 82.5 years]{.claim id="c002"}. The
robust trend estimate points to [an increase of about 0.30 years per calendar year, an increasing trend (Theil-Sen, Mann-Kendall)]{.claim id="c017"}.
The EU average, available since the start of the century, rose more slowly:
[about 0.16 years per year, also an increasing trend]{.claim id="c018"}.

Portugal moved from slightly below the European average, with [77.4 years in 2002]{.claim id="c004"}
against [77.6 years in the EU]{.claim id="c003"}, to above it: [82.5 years]{.claim id="c002"} against
[81.5 years in the EU in 2024]{.claim id="c005"}, [a difference of 1.0 year in Portugal's favour]{.claim id="c006"}.

Women live longer than men. At the start of the series, life expectancy at birth was
[66.7 years for women in 1960]{.claim id="c009"} and [61.1 years for men]{.claim id="c010"};
at the end it was [85.2 years for women in 2024]{.claim id="c007"} and [79.7 years for men]{.claim id="c008"}.

[At age 65, life expectancy rose from 13.6 years in 1960]{.claim id="c011"} to
[21.1 years in 2024]{.claim id="c012"}, above the European average ([20.2 years in 2024]{.claim id="c013"}).

In the first years of the pandemic the series fell back: from [82.0 years in 2019]{.claim id="c014"} to
[81.4 years in 2020]{.claim id="c015"} and [81.4 years in 2021]{.claim id="c016"}. The break detector
did not classify this dip as a level break, and the study does not attribute a cause to it.

```{ojs}
le_data = FileAttachment("q01_life_expectancy.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof le_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof le_age = Inputs.radio(new Map([["At birth", "0"], ["At 65", "65"]]), {value: "0", label: "Age"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, le_data.filter((d) => d.sex === le_sex && String(d.age) === le_age), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Life expectancy (years)", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth and at sixty-five, Portugal and EU (Eurostat).*

### Regional differences

INE regional data are computed over three-year periods, and each point corresponds to the period
starting in the year shown. In the most recent period in the series, life expectancy at birth
ranged from [78.04 years in the Autonomous Region of the Azores]{.claim id="c020"} to
[81.53 years in the Norte]{.claim id="c019"}, with [Madeira at 78.77 years]{.claim id="c022"}. The
autonomous regions remain at the bottom of the table but are rising the fastest: the Azores started
from [75.86 years in the period beginning in 2008]{.claim id="c021"}, with
[an increasing trend of about 0.21 years per year]{.claim id="c023"}. In the Algarve the series
[shows no clear trend]{.claim id="c024"}.

```{ojs}
ler_data = FileAttachment("q01_life_expectancy_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, ler_data, {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Life expectancy at birth (years)", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth by NUTS II region (former nomenclature), three-year periods, INE.*

## Question 2 — Healthy life years

Healthy life years (years without activity limitation reported in the EU-SILC survey) in Portugal
grew from [53.9 years at birth in 2004]{.claim id="c025"} to
[64.8 years in 2024]{.claim id="c026"}. In the EU they went from [62.9]{.claim id="c027"} to
[65.2 years]{.claim id="c028"} over the same period. The gap with the EU narrowed from
[9.0 years in 2004]{.claim id="c029"} to [0.4 years in 2024]{.claim id="c030"}.

The Portuguese series is, however, very irregular. The trend test
[finds no clear trend (estimated slope of about 0.12 years per year, not significant after correction)]{.claim id="c036"},
largely because of an isolated trough in the middle of the last decade, which may be a survey
artefact ([see Breaks and events]{.claim id="c206"}).

[At 65, healthy life years rose from 4.4 in 2004]{.claim id="c031"} to
[9.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c032"}, [with an increasing trend]{.claim id="c037"}, now close to the European
average ([10.3 years in 2024]{.claim id="c033"}). The share of healthy years in total life
expectancy rose from [68.7% in 2004]{.claim id="c034"} to [78.6% in 2024]{.claim id="c035"}.

Although they live longer, women do not live more years without limitations. In the latest year
the estimate was [63.9 healthy life years for women in 2024]{.claim id="c038"} and
[65.8 years for men]{.claim id="c039"}, which means women spend more years with limitations.

```{ojs}
hly_data = FileAttachment("q02_healthy_life_years.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof hly_ind = Inputs.select(new Map([["Healthy life years at birth", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_Y0"], ["Healthy life years at 65", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_Y65"], ["Share of life expectancy at birth (%)", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_LE_Y0_PC"], ["Share of life expectancy at 65 (%)", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_LE_Y65_PC"]]), {label: "Indicator"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof hly_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, hly_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === hly_ind && d.sex === hly_sex), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: hly_ind.endsWith("_PC") ? "% of life expectancy" : "Years", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: healthy life years and share of life expectancy, Portugal and EU (Eurostat).*

## Question 3 — Causes of death

Eurostat's age-standardised rates allow Portugal to be compared with the EU. Mortality from
diseases of the circulatory system fell from [321.67 per hundred thousand in 2011]{.claim id="c040"}
to [220.81 in 2023]{.claim id="c041"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 7.2 deaths per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c055"}. It stayed
well below the European average ([312.95 in 2023]{.claim id="c042"}).

For malignant neoplasms, the rate went from [246.73 in 2011]{.claim id="c043"} to
[218.22 in 2023]{.claim id="c044"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 1.4 deaths per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c056"}, below the EU
([233.13]{.claim id="c045"}). Diabetes nearly halved, from
[44.60 in 2011]{.claim id="c048"} to [23.71 in 2023]{.claim id="c049"}, practically at the European
level ([23.53]{.claim id="c050"}).

Respiratory diseases are the main exception: [95.48 per hundred thousand in Portugal]{.claim id="c046"}
against [75.18 in the EU in 2023]{.claim id="c047"}. External causes (accidents, falls, suicide,
among others) [show no clear trend]{.claim id="c057"} and stood at
[45.24 per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c051"}, against [49.40 in the EU]{.claim id="c052"}. Taking all
causes together, Portugal recorded [885.63 deaths per hundred thousand in 2023]{.claim id="c053"}, below the EU
([963.42]{.claim id="c054"}).

All these series show a simultaneous and unusually sharp drop in the same recent year, which
probably reflects a change of method rather than a real change
([see Limitations]{.claim id="c203"}).

```{ojs}
cpe_data = FileAttachment("q03_causes_pt_eu.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof cpe_cause = Inputs.select(new Map([["All causes", "all_causes"], ["Circulatory system", "circulatory"], ["Malignant neoplasms", "cancer_C00_C97"], ["Respiratory system", "respiratory"], ["Diabetes", "diabetes"], ["External causes", "external_causes"]]), {label: "Cause"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof cpe_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, cpe_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === cpe_cause && d.sex === cpe_sex), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants (standardised rate)", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: standardised death rate by cause, Portugal and EU (Eurostat).*

### Regional differences

INE data under the new regional nomenclature use a different standard population from Eurostat's,
so the levels cannot be compared with those in the previous chart. In this series, Portugal had
[863.9 deaths per hundred thousand in 2024 (all causes)]{.claim id="c060"}. The Autonomous Region of
the Azores stands out with [1161.9]{.claim id="c058"}, followed by the [Alentejo with 1011.6]{.claim id="c063"}.
Grande Lisboa had the lowest rate ([820.3]{.claim id="c059"}). For diseases of the circulatory system,
the Azores ([266.9 per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c061"}) almost doubled the Norte
([154.9]{.claim id="c062"}).


```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, creg_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === creg_cause && d.sex === "T"), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants (standardised rate)", events: linked_events, lang})
```

### Premature mortality

The premature mortality rate (between thirty and seventy, from cardiovascular disease, cancer,
diabetes and chronic respiratory disease) fell from [357.5 per hundred thousand in 2002]{.claim id="c064"} to
[267.9 in 2024]{.claim id="c065"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 2.0 per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c067"}. Among men
([370.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c068"}) it is more than double that of women
([173.3]{.claim id="c069"}). The lowest value in the series was recorded in
[2020, at 258.5]{.claim id="c066"}.

[The standardised death rate before age 75, all causes, was 320.0 per hundred thousand in 2019]{.claim id="c070"}; it rose to [338.9 in 2021]{.claim id="c071"} and fell again
to [302.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c072"}. This is one of the few indirect signs of the impact of the
pandemic available in these data.

```{ojs}
pm_data = FileAttachment("q03_premature_mortality.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof pm_ind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Premature (ages 30-70)", "premature_mortality_rate_30_70"], ["Before age 75 (standardised)", "standardised_mortality_rate_under75"]]), {value: "premature_mortality_rate_30_70", label: "Indicator"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, pm_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === pm_ind), {groupBy: "sex", labels: {HM: "Total", H: "Men", M: "Women"}, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: premature mortality and standardised mortality before seventy-five, Portugal (INE).*

## Question 4 — Avoidable mortality and infant mortality

Treatable mortality (deaths that timely and effective health care could avoid) fell from
[94.78 per hundred thousand in 2011]{.claim id="c073"} to [74.24 in 2023]{.claim id="c074"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 1.8 per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c080"}, and is below the EU
average ([86.81]{.claim id="c075"}).

Preventable mortality (deaths avoidable through prevention and public health) went from
[149.25 in 2011]{.claim id="c076"} to [125.94 in 2023]{.claim id="c077"}, but the test
[finds no clear trend]{.claim id="c081"}: there was a peak in
[2021, at 155.89]{.claim id="c079"}. The European average is higher ([150.85 in 2023]{.claim id="c078"}).
The loaded data contain only Portugal and the EU aggregate, which does not allow Portugal to be
ranked among the Member States.

```{ojs}
av_data = FileAttachment("q04_avoidable_mortality.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof av_ind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Treatable", "treatable"], ["Preventable", "preventable"]]), {value: "treatable", label: "Type"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof av_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, av_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === av_ind && d.sex === av_sex), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: avoidable mortality (preventable and treatable), Portugal and EU (Eurostat).*

Infant mortality is one of the largest transformations in the series: from
[77.5 deaths per thousand live births in 1960]{.claim id="c082"} to [3.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c083"}, with
[a decreasing trend]{.claim id="c088"}. The minimum was [2.4 in 2020]{.claim id="c085"}, and the most
recent value is below the EU average ([3.5 in 2024]{.claim id="c084"}). Neonatal mortality followed the
same path, from [27.9 in 1960]{.claim id="c086"} to [1.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c087"}.

With such small annual numbers, INE publishes a five-year rate for the regions. In the most recent
five-year period, Portugal recorded [2.7 deaths per thousand live births (five-year period ending in 2025)]{.claim id="c089"}.
The [Centro had 2.1]{.claim id="c090"} and the [Alentejo 2.9]{.claim id="c091"}.

```{ojs}

```

```{ojs}

```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, inf_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === inf_ind), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 1,000 live births", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: infant, neonatal and perinatal mortality, Portugal and EU (Eurostat; the EU has only the infant rate).*



*Chart: five-year infant mortality rate by region, most recent period (INE).*

## Question 5 — Excess mortality during the pandemic

This question was not answered. Both planned Eurostat sources failed the access test.
Weekly deaths by region [exceeded the test time limit without returning a result]{.claim id="c092"},
and monthly excess mortality [returned a server error]{.claim id="c093"}. By a decision recorded
in the study, the analysis proceeded without this component and
[weekly excess mortality is declared as not covered]{.claim id="c094"}. The only indirect signs in
these data are the dip in life expectancy at the start of the pandemic and the temporary rise in
mortality before seventy-five (Question 1 and Question 3).

## Question 6 — Morbidity and self-rated health

The share of people aged sixteen or over reporting a chronic disease or long-standing health problem
rose from [32.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c095"} to [44.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c096"},
[an increasing trend of about 0.7 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c097"}. Part of this rise is
concentrated in a single jump that coincides with a new wave of the European health survey and is
probably methodological ([see Breaks and events]{.claim id="c204"}). By region, the highest values
are in [Madeira (47.5% in 2025)]{.claim id="c098"} and the
[Centro (46.8%)]{.claim id="c099"}, and the lowest in the [Algarve (38.5%)]{.claim id="c100"}.

At the same time, self-rated health improved. According to INE, the share rating their health as
bad or very bad fell from [21.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c101"} to [12.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c102"}
([a decreasing trend]{.claim id="c107"}), and the share rating it good or very good rose from
[45.4%]{.claim id="c103"} to [52.7%]{.claim id="c104"}. The improvement is largest among older people: the
share with bad or very bad health [among people aged 65 or over went from 55.2% in 2004]{.claim id="c105"}
to [28.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c106"}.

More reported chronic disease and better self-rating can coexist, for instance with more diagnoses
and better-controlled conditions, but these data do not allow the explanations to be told apart.

In the European comparison (EU-SILC), Portugal still lags behind. In the latest year,
[52.6% of Portuguese people rated their health as good or very good in 2025]{.claim id="c108"}, against
[67.9% in the EU]{.claim id="c109"}, and [12.2% as bad or very bad]{.claim id="c110"}, against
[8.8% in the EU]{.claim id="c111"}. In Portugal the latter share was [20.3% in 2010]{.claim id="c112"},
with [a decreasing trend of about 0.5 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c113"}.

## Question 7 — Risk factors

Risk factor data come from the National Health Survey. Tobacco and body mass index exist only for
the most recent wave, and alcohol has three waves. The loaded data contain no EU comparison and no
information on physical activity.

[In 2025, 12.7% of the population aged fifteen or over smoked daily]{.claim id="c114"}. Among men
the share was [17.3%]{.claim id="c115"} and among women [8.4%]{.claim id="c116"}. The
[Algarve (18.2%)]{.claim id="c117"} and the [Azores (18.1%)]{.claim id="c118"} had the highest shares,
and the [Centro (10.5%)]{.claim id="c119"} the lowest. About
[61.9% of the population had never smoked]{.claim id="c120"}.

Obesity affected [17.4% of adults in 2025]{.claim id="c121"}.

Among those who drank alcohol in the previous twelve months, the share with at least one occasion
of six or more drinks rose from [33.2% in 2014]{.claim id="c122"} to [42.8% in 2019]{.claim id="c123"}
and stood at [42.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c124"}. Among young people [aged 15 to 24 it went from 45.7% in 2014]{.claim id="c125"}
to [66.2% in 2025]{.claim id="c126"}. With only three waves, no trend test is carried out.

```{ojs}
smk_data = FileAttachment("q07_daily_smokers_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof smk_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "HM"], ["Men", "H"], ["Women", "M"]]), {value: "HM", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
ranking(Plotly, dedupe(smk_data.filter((d) => d.sex === smk_sex), (d) => d.region), {xTitle: "% daily smokers (aged fifteen or over)", highlight: "Portugal", lang})
```

*Chart: daily smokers by region and sex (INE, National Health Survey).*

```{ojs}
tob_data = FileAttachment("q07_tobacco.json").json()
```

## Question 8 — Mental health

The longest comparable series is suicide. The rate was
[11.6 per hundred thousand inhabitants in 2002]{.claim id="c127"}, reached [11.7 in 2014]{.claim id="c128"} and
stood at [9.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c129"}; the test [finds no clear trend]{.claim id="c130"}.
Among men the rate is more than three times that of women ([15.5]{.claim id="c131"} against
[4.4 in 2022]{.claim id="c132"}). Among people aged seventy-five or over, the rate fell from
[33.5 in 2002]{.claim id="c133"} to [20.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c134"}. The national series joins two
INE tables (former nomenclature up to one year, new nomenclature afterwards), and the splice may
affect comparability.

For depressive symptoms, the share of people without symptoms fell from
[88.7% in 2014]{.claim id="c135"} to [83.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c136"}, and the share with severe
symptoms went from [3.7%]{.claim id="c137"} to [4.3%]{.claim id="c138"}. With three waves and
different survey methods, this is an indication and not a demonstrated trend. Antidepressant
consumption and the mental health modules of the European survey were not part of the loaded data.

## Question 9 — Unmet needs for care

Unmet needs here are those due to cost, distance or waiting list. For medical care, the share in
Portugal went from [1.1% in 2008]{.claim id="c139"} to [3.3% in 2012]{.claim id="c140"}, in the crisis
years, and stood at [2.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c141"}, close to the European average
([2.4%]{.claim id="c142"}). Over the full series
[there is no clear trend]{.claim id="c154"}.

For dental care, the problem is larger: [7.3% in 2008]{.claim id="c143"}, a peak of
[14.6% in 2015]{.claim id="c144"} and [7.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c145"}, against
[3.3% in the EU]{.claim id="c146"}. Here too [there is no clear trend over the full series]{.claim id="c155"}.

Inequality by income is very marked. In the lowest income quintile, unmet dental needs reached
[27.6% in 2015]{.claim id="c147"} and stood at
[16.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c148"}, against [1.6% in the highest quintile]{.claim id="c149"}. For medical
care, they were [4.2% in the lowest quintile]{.claim id="c150"} and [1.0% in the highest in 2025]{.claim id="c151"}.
Among those below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold the total share was
[7.5%]{.claim id="c152"}, against [3.3% above the threshold]{.claim id="c153"}.

## Question 10 — Health system expenditure and resources

Current health expenditure rose from [8.62% of GDP in 2000]{.claim id="c156"} to a peak of
[11.22% in 2021]{.claim id="c157"} and stood at [10.20% in 2024]{.claim id="c158"}, at the EU level
([10.16%]{.claim id="c159"}). Per inhabitant, in purchasing power standards, Portugal spent
[3247.42 in 2024]{.claim id="c160"}, against [4074.88 in the EU]{.claim id="c161"}.

The financing structure sets Portugal apart. Household out-of-pocket payments accounted for
[28.67% of current expenditure in 2024]{.claim id="c162"}, almost double the EU
([15.06%]{.claim id="c163"}), and their share shows [an increasing trend of about 0.23 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c166"}.
Government and compulsory financing covered [61.88%]{.claim id="c164"}, against
[80.33% in the EU]{.claim id="c165"}.

The number of physicians licensed to practise went from
[75.65 per hundred thousand inhabitants in 1960]{.claim id="c167"} to [591.35 in 2024]{.claim id="c168"}. This
concept includes physicians who do not practise and overestimates active physicians. Practising
nurses went from [422.29 in 2004]{.claim id="c169"} to [767.54 in 2024]{.claim id="c170"}. Both
series have jumps that suggest changes of definition ([see Limitations]{.claim id="c205"}).

Hospital beds fell from [395.92 per hundred thousand in 1985]{.claim id="c171"} to
[330.98 in 2024]{.claim id="c172"}, well below the European average ([507.35]{.claim id="c173"}).
Differences between regions are large. In the latest available year, the Norte had
[561.01 physicians per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c174"} and the Alentejo [322.33]{.claim id="c175"}; Madeira had
[793.69 beds per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c176"} and the Alentejo [213.18]{.claim id="c177"}.

## Breaks and events

Automatic detection looked for changes in level, changes in slope and isolated spikes in the main
series. It found [51 candidate breaks, of which 18 were linked to a dated event, all grade C, and 33 were left without an event]{.claim id="c202"}.
No source consulted establishes that any of these events caused a change in the series, so the
text speaks only of coincidence in time. Links to national legal acts are not described here,
because the text of their source pages could not be confirmed; only events and links with a
verified source are presented.

### Events considered

- [The Memorandum of Understanding with the European Commission, the ECB and the IMF ran from May 2011 to May 2014 and included health spending containment measures]{.claim id="c179"}.
- [The World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 pandemic on 11 March 2020]{.claim id="c180"}.
- [The 2014/2015 winter had a severe influenza season in Europe, with excess mortality among older people]{.claim id="c184"}.

### Links found (all grade C)

- [The 2012 change in the life expectancy gap with the EU coincided with the first full year of the adjustment programme]{.claim id="c187"}.
- [The 2011 spike in the share of people with bad or very bad health, and in the gap with the EU, coincided with the start of the adjustment programme]{.claim id="c193"}.
- [The 2012 spike in the gap in unmet dental needs with the EU coincided with the adjustment programme]{.claim id="c196"}.
- [The 2015 change in unmet medical needs relative to the EU, one year after the end of the programme, coincided with the post-programme period]{.claim id="c199"}.
- [The 2021 drop in standardised mortality from circulatory diseases coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c188"},
  but its size suggests a change of method.
- [The 2021 drop in mortality from respiratory diseases coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c189"};
  COVID is coded as a separate cause.
- [The 2021 slope change in preventable mortality coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c190"}.
- [The unusually low 2020 value in premature mortality coincided with the first year of the pandemic]{.claim id="c192"}.
- [The 2020 change in the gap in bad or very bad health relative to the EU coincided with the first year of the pandemic]{.claim id="c194"}.
- [The 2020 change in the gap in dental needs relative to the EU coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c198"}.
- [The 2020 rise in health expenditure as a percentage of GDP coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c200"};
  that year GDP, the denominator, also fell.
- [The one-off 2020 drop in the share of out-of-pocket payments coincided with the pandemic]{.claim id="c201"}.

### Breaks without an event and events without an effect

These cases are results of the analysis, not failures. [Left without an identified event were, among others, the breaks of 1972, 1975 and 2005 in life expectancy, of 1961 and 1975 in infant mortality, of 1985 in perinatal mortality, of 2016 in external causes and treatable mortality, of 2000 in hospital beds and of 2010 in out-of-pocket payments]{.claim id="c208"}.
In several cases the most likely explanation is technical rather than an event:

- [The simultaneous 2021 drop in all Eurostat standardised rates suggests a change of method or of standard population]{.claim id="c203"}, not confirmed by a source.
- [The 2014 and 2019 jumps in chronic disease and self-rated health coincide with new waves of the European health survey and are probably series breaks]{.claim id="c204"}.
- [The size of the 2010 jump in physicians and the 2014 jump in nurses suggests changes of definition]{.claim id="c205"}.
- [The 2014 trough in healthy life years may be a survey artefact]{.claim id="c206"}.

[The severe 2014/2015 influenza season does not coincide with any life expectancy break in the series analysed and was recorded as an event without visible effect]{.claim id="c207"}.

## Associations between indicators

Spearman correlations were tested between the annual changes of pairs of national series from
different charts, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Using annual differences
avoids two series appearing associated only because both rise over time.
[45 pairs were tested and none remained significant after correction]{.claim id="c209"}. This
is a result: there are no robust associations between indicators in these data. Even if there were,
they would be associations and not causes, and some could be mechanical, for example between a part
and its total.

## Methodology

- **Data.** All series come from INE and Eurostat tables, downloaded by code and normalised to a
  long format (date, region, sex, age, indicator, value, unit) in `data/clean/`. National Health
  Survey proportions (tobacco, body mass index, alcohol, depressive symptoms) were computed as the
  count in the category divided by the total of the same table.
- **Trends.** The annual slope is estimated with the Theil-Sen estimator, which is robust to
  outliers. Significance is tested with Mann-Kendall and corrected for multiple testing. The text
  only says "increasing" or "decreasing trend" when the test confirms it; otherwise it says "no
  clear trend".
- **Breaks.** Changes in level and slope were detected with the PELT algorithm, and isolated spikes
  with a robust z-score. For each break a dated event with a primary source was sought within a
  plausible window. The grade of evidence (A, B or C) determines the wording used.
- **EU comparison.** The Eurostat aggregate of the twenty-seven Member States is used whenever it
  exists in the loaded data.
- **Regions.** Regional series use the NUTS nomenclature in which the source publishes them. The
  new nomenclature splits the former Lisbon Metropolitan Area and redraws the Centro and the
  Alentejo, so series from the two nomenclatures appear in separate charts.

## Limitations

- **Excess mortality not covered.** By a decision recorded in the study,
  [weekly excess mortality was not covered]{.claim id="c094"}: the weekly deaths source
  [exceeded the test time limit]{.claim id="c092"} and the monthly excess mortality source
  [returned a server error]{.claim id="c093"}. Question 5 remains unanswered.
- **Method break in a recent year.** Eurostat's standardised rates by cause all fall at the same
  time in that year, which is inconsistent with a pandemic effect and suggests a change of method
  ([see Breaks and events]{.claim id="c203"}). Changes between the start of the series and that
  year should be read with caution.
- **National and European sources are not directly comparable.** INE and Eurostat standardised
  rates use different standard populations.
- **Surveys with series breaks.** Chronic disease, self-rated health and healthy life years depend
  on surveys with method changes ([see Breaks and events]{.claim id="c204"}).
  National Health Survey indicators have few waves (tobacco and body mass index only one), which
  rules out trend tests and EU comparison.
- **Health personnel.** Physicians are counted as "licensed to practise", which overestimates
  active physicians, and the series have jumps that appear definitional
  ([see Breaks and events]{.claim id="c205"}).
- **Scope not covered.** No data were loaded on antidepressant consumption, the mental health
  modules of the European survey, physical activity, life expectancy by education level, or
  Portugal's position among the Member States (only the EU aggregate). Socioeconomic inequalities
  were analysed only by income, for unmet needs.
- **Spliced suicide series.** The national series joins two INE tables with different regional
  nomenclatures.
- **Provisional values.** The most recent years of several Eurostat series may be revised.
